subject: psychiatry
title: Classification Systems and Mental Status Examination

steps.tx: **International Classification of Diseases 11th Revision** serves as the global diagnostic standard published by the World Health Organization, while the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision provides criteria primarily in North America. Both frameworks categorize psychiatric conditions into dimensional and categorical clusters based on validated symptom duration and functional impairment.
steps.say: International psychiatric nosology relies on ICD-11 globally and DSM-5-TR in specialized practice. Both classification systems group mental disorders through structured clinical criteria and functional severity thresholds.

steps.tx: **Mental status examination** provides a structured cross-sectional clinical evaluation of a patient's psychological functioning at the precise time of the psychiatric interview. Systematic evaluation covers general appearance and behavior, speech characteristics, mood and affect, thought form and content, perceptual abnormalities, cognitive faculties including orientation, and insight into illness.
steps.say: The mental status examination systematically documents patient behavior, speech, emotional state, thought processes, perception, and cognitive faculties observed during the interview.

vis.title: MSE Systematic Domains
rows: Grooming, hygiene, eye contact, motor activity
Pressure of speech or poverty of speech
Sustained emotional tone vs immediate display

steps.tx: The mental state examination begins before a single question is asked. **General appearance and psychomotor behaviour** record grooming, eye contact, agitation or retardation, and odd movements in plain observable language. A slowed patient who answers in monosyllables and a pacing patient who cannot sit are already telling diagnostic stories. Writing what is seen, rather than what is inferred, keeps this first section useful to every clinician who reads it later.
steps.say: Appearance and psychomotor behaviour open the mental state examination with observed facts. Plain description keeps the record useful to later readers.

vis.caption: A clinician observes grooming, posture and movement during a psychiatric interview. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **General appearance and psychomotor behavior** provides immediate diagnostic clues regarding personal self-care, nutritional status, level of consciousness, and psychomotor activity. Severe depression classically causes psychomotor retardation with stooped posture and poverty of movement, whereas acute manic episodes present with hyperactive, intrusive behavior and colorful, eccentric attire.
steps.say: Initial observation captures dress, personal cleanliness, nutritional status, and movement patterns. Psychomotor slowing characterizes severe depression, whereas mania produces uninhibited motor restlessness.

steps.tx: **Affective congruence** describes whether an observed emotional expression aligns logically with the patient's stated mood and underlying thought content. Mood denotes a pervasive, sustained emotional climate experienced subjectively, while affect reflects the momentary, observable emotional reactivity manifested through facial expression, vocal pitch, and communicative gestures.
steps.say: Mood represents the patient's sustained internal emotional climate, while affect is the examiner's objective observation of momentary emotional expression and responsiveness.

right.title: Observed Affect
points: Observed through facial cues and tone

steps.tx: **Insight grading** assesses the patient's awareness of their psychiatric illness, graded systematically across six recognized levels from complete denial to true emotional insight. Grade one denotes complete denial of illness, grade two recognizes need for help while denying sickness, while grade six exhibits true emotional insight enabling treatment adherence.
steps.say: Insight progresses through six distinct levels, from complete denial of any illness up to mature emotional understanding that motivates voluntary therapeutic cooperation.

nodes.label: Grade 1: Complete denial of any illness or disturbance
Grade 2: Slight awareness of needing help while denying sickness
Grade 3: Awareness of being sick while attributing it to external causes
Grade 4: Awareness that illness stems from internal unknown causes
Grade 5: Intellectual insight with intellectual awareness but no behavioral change
Grade 6: True emotional insight with therapeutic compliance and lifestyle adaptation

steps.tx: **Cognitive orientation** testing evaluates awareness of time, place, and person, which is typically preserved in functional psychoses but impaired early in organic delirium and advanced neurocognitive disorders. Attention and concentration are tested through serial sevens subtraction or spelling backwards, assessing frontoparietal working memory circuits.
steps.say: Orientation to time, place, and person remains intact in purely functional psychoses but fails in delirium. Serial subtractions and backward spelling assess active working concentration.

vis.title: Cognitive Domain Tests
rows: Date, day, hospital ward, city, identity
Digit span forward, month names backward
Three words recalled after five minutes

steps.tx: **Psychiatric interview techniques** employ open-ended exploration followed by targeted closed questioning, maintaining non-judgmental neutrality and empathetic listening to build therapeutic rapport. Clinicians carefully distinguish neurosis, where reality testing remains intact without bizarre hallucinations, from psychosis, where fundamental loss of reality contact and unshakeable delusions dominate.
steps.say: The psychiatric interview relies on non-judgmental, empathetic open questioning. Reality testing distinguishes neuroses like anxiety from psychoses like schizophrenia.

right.title: Psychotic Disorders
points: Insight is lost or significantly impaired

steps.tx: **Judgement assessment** evaluates the patient's capacity to comprehend situations realistically, foresee potential consequences, and undertake appropriate constructive actions. Clinicians test personal judgment by discussing social and occupational life decisions, and test hypothetical judgment using standard scenarios such as discovering a stamped envelope on a sidewalk.
steps.say: Judgement reflects the capacity to anticipate consequences and choose realistic actions. It is evaluated through life choices and standardized hypothetical scenarios.

nodes.label: Present structured hypothetical scenario to patient
Evaluate logical appraisal and consideration of safety
Compare with actual real-world decision-making history
Determine capacity for independent community living and legal decisions
